newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--10-yr T-note sale, Beige Book.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--10-yr T-note sale, Beige Book.

text.p: The Treasury's sale of $12.0 billion 10-year notes, followed by the afternoon release of the Federal Reserve's anecdotal description of business conditions around the country, will highlight Wednesday's U.S. government securities trading session, analysts said.
The 10-year note sale is the last leg of the two-part quarterly refunding; the Treasury sold $17.0 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday.
The Beige Book could report a slight slowing in the economy, some analysts said.
Reports on March wholesale inventories, March consumer credit and first quarter productivity and unit labor costs are also due on Wednesday.
A three-year note auction on Tuesday that disappointed the market "leaves the burden on the 10-year auction," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
Stiles said some players will be tempted to "get involved with the 10-year notes on a speculative basis because the retail sales data (due next week) looks like it will be weak."
If the retail sales data are weak, the 10-year notes could appreciate and then those players could take profits, he said.
Some analysts said the 10-year auction could attract demand from bidders who want to lengthen the average durations of their portfolios.
Stiles was skeptical of that potential scenario.
"You'll hear talk of a strong bid to shore up durations but that will be hype," he said. "In reality, it will just be a spec play."

Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said the biggest change likely to be reflected in the Fed's Beige Book from the last such report will probably lie in the description of the economy's retail sector.
"Sales in April were very, very poor and the (Beige Book) should mirror that," said Schaja. "Auto sales were off a lot so that should be reflected as well," she said.

But the Beige Book is not likely to persuade people in one direction or another in terms of interpreting the next Fed policy move. She said the Fed's description of the economy was likely to characterize the labor market as tight but, in line with the first-quarter Employment Cost Index reading, showing no significant wage pressures.

With regard the other economic reports that the market will get on Wednesday, first-quarter productivity and unit labor costs data, expected at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, are forecast to show a 2.4 percent productivity rise with a 1.0 percent unit labor cost increase, said economists polled by Reuters.
In the fourth quarter, productivity rose 1.1 percent and and unit labor costs jumped 2.5 percent.
The March wholesale inventories report, also due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, should show that inventories rose 0.4 percent in March after staying flat in February, economists said.
Economists believe that Federal Reserve data on consumer installment credit remained steady at $6.7 billion in March.
"We're not going to react to that," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.
The 30-year Treasury bond ended at 96-22/32 on Tuesday, yielding 6.89 percent.
In when-issued trade, the 10-year Treasury notes set for auction on Wednesday, finished with a 6.6775 percent yield.
